narrative:
The 2023 Detroit Tigers entered the season with cautious optimism, hoping that a blend of young talent and veteran presence could push them toward playoff relevance. Instead, April proved to be a brutal reality check. The bullpen — particularly Alex Lange — was already showing cracks, and a 10-16 record left the Tigers buried near the bottom of the AL Central before May even arrived. The lone bright spot was a stunning three-run homer from Nick Maton on April 14th that briefly sparked life, but the month was defined more by blown leads and poor relief appearances than any sustainable momentum.

May brought a genuine resurgence. The Tigers rattled off a 16-11 record, their best month of the season, fueled by clutch moments up and down the lineup. Jake Rogers launched a grand slam, Akil Baddoo delivered another, Eric Haase came through in the clutch, and Riley Greene began flashing the star potential that made him so exciting. It was messy, imperfect baseball — a team winning ugly — but it was winning. For a few weeks in May, Detroit looked like a team that might actually claw its way back into the race.

June and July told a grimmer story. A dismal 9-18 June collapse, punctuated by Jason Foley's catastrophic meltdown against Arizona that swung nearly three-quarters of a win in a single play, sent the Tigers reeling. Even a 12-13 July record couldn't fully mask the sense that this team was treading water. The offense sputtered, the bullpen remained unreliable, and a playoff push felt increasingly like a fantasy. Kerry Carpenter continued to provide heroic moments, but they were increasingly lonely bright spots in a losing effort.

August and September told two very different stories. August opened with more inconsistency, but late in the month something clicked — Parker Meadows hit his first career home run, Kerry Carpenter delivered a grand slam, and Javier Báez flashed the spark that had been missing all year. September became the season's most joyful chapter, an 18-10 record that was equal parts too little, too late and genuine promise for the future. The Tigers finished 78-84, short of the playoffs, but the September surge offered a tantalizing glimpse of what this young core might become in 2024.

chapters.title: April Stumbles
chapters.description: A rocky start defined by bullpen failures and a 10-16 record, with rare offensive fireworks unable to mask Detroit's early-season struggles.

chapters.title: May Surge
chapters.description: The Tigers caught fire in May, going 16-11 on the backs of grand slams, clutch hits, and a young lineup that finally started delivering.

chapters.title: June Collapse
chapters.description: A catastrophic 9-18 June buried any playoff hopes, as the bullpen imploded and costly losses piled up at the worst possible time.

chapters.title: Treading Water
chapters.description: July and early August produced a .500-ish grind — flashes of brilliance from Torkelson and Vierling mixed with more bullpen heartbreak.

chapters.title: Late-Season Sparks
chapters.description: Kerry Carpenter's grand slam, Parker Meadows' first homer, and a Báez clutch single ignited a late August charge that hinted at what was coming.

chapters.title: September Statement
chapters.description: An 18-10 September run — the Tigers' best stretch of the year — arrived too late for the playoffs but sent a clear message about the future of this young club.
